# Pure Domain Engine Shared Across Hosts

Keep the rules of the domain in one UI-free, platform-free module, and let each host — a browser
simulator, a phone, a test harness — supply only *input* and *display*. The engine does not know which
one it is running in.

In [[farely]] this is `apps/tester/src/app/lib/`: `engine`, `coordinator`, `controls`, `events`,
`liveEvents`, `vision`, `diagnostics`, `diagStore`, `carLookup`, `device`, `session`, `theme`,
`bridge`. The **same built bundle** is served by Vite in the browser and loaded by the
[[capacitor]] WebView inside the APK — `capacitor.config.json` points `webDir` straight at
`../tester/dist`. The native side is described as only capturing and displaying.

## What the split buys

- **The unbuilt half stays testable.** Every offer-scoring rule in {{deadhead-adjusted-net-profit}}
  could be exercised in a browser long before an APK existed — which, given that Farely never ran on a
  live shift, is the only reason any of it was exercised at all. The simulator was the product for its
  whole life.
- **One implementation, not two.** No native scoring path exists to drift from the JS one. Contrast
  the sibling product [[stickfps]], which deliberately duplicated its simulation code across hosts
  instead.
- **The native boundary stays small.** ~1,099 lines of Kotlin against ~12,100 lines of TypeScript. The
  Kotlin does capture ([[accessibility-service-overlay]]) and drawing
  ([[accessibility-overlay-over-system-alert-window]]); it makes no money decisions.

## The seam

A Capacitor plugin bridge in both directions: `FarelyBridgePlugin.emitRawOffer` pushes a `RawOffer`
into the WebView, `showOverlay` sends the verdict back out. The data crossing is small and dumb —
strings and numbers off the node tree — which is what keeps the engine platform-free. `offerFromRaw()`
on the JS side does all the normalising (fuzzy Polish place resolution, estimating missing km/min,
setting the `approx` flag), so the native side never has to know the domain.

## Where the purity is imperfect

`vision.ts` reaches the network directly and switches transport by host — `CapacitorHttp` natively, a
Vite dev proxy in the browser, direct `fetch` otherwise. So the "pure" library does contain host
detection, isolated to the one module that must do I/O. `device.ts` likewise sniffs RAM to pick a LITE
tier. Both are honest exceptions rather than leaks scattered through the engine.

## Cost paid

A duplicated mirror elsewhere: `apps/android/reference/` is a **hand-maintained copy** of the Kotlin
files, which CONTRIBUTING asks the developer to keep in sync manually. The discipline that removed
duplication from the domain layer did not reach the native layer.
